主要内容: Despite positive signs in the U.S. housing market, such as easing price gains and improving employment, home prices remain too high for many buyers. According to Jed Kolko, chief economist at Trulia, 97 out of 100 metropolitan housing markets saw year-over-year price increases in June 2014, the highest since the recovery began. Asking prices rose by 1.2% month-over-month, the highest in 16 months. However, affordability remains a major issue, with home sales still below 2013 levels. Real estate agents report that sellers are out of touch with what buyers can afford, leading to bidding wars. Nela Richardson, chief economist at Redfin, noted that 40% of sellers planned to list their homes above market value in May 2014, despite a 9% drop in home sales since the previous year. Mortgage applications for existing homes fell 10% year-over-year, and applications for new homes dropped 5% in June. The Federal Reserve highlighted that restrictive credit conditions, particularly for low-credit-score households, high down payments, and student loan debt, are dampening housing demand. Affordability concerns also extend to the rental market, where rents are rising and taking a larger share of paychecks. Despite positive signs in the U.S. housing market, rent prices remain too high for many renters. In 25 of the largest rental markets, rent increases have outpaced wage increases, with some areas seeing rent rises of over 10 percent year-over-year. For example, in Miami, FL, rent for a 2-bedroom apartment is 10.1% of the average local wage, while in San Francisco, CA, it is 13.8%. These high rent-to-income ratios make home ownership unattainable for many, even though mortgage rates have dropped. The debt-to-income ratio, which limits loan debt to 43% of a borrower's income, has kept some renters from buying homes. In 8 of the 10 largest housing markets, the median rent as a share of the local wage exceeds 43%, with some areas seeing rents over half of the average wage. This situation highlights the ongoing affordability crisis in the U.S. housing market.
